Green beans, Doctors, Pharmacists and Drug Dens

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Drug dens are expanding their offering to include mood altering and psyhotrophic schedule 5 medicines. We investigate who the doctors and pharmacies are behind the trend.

Summary:
Stilpaine is known in the northern areas of PE as "green beans." The schedule 5 pain killer is in high demand. A few tablets taken with alcohol is reportedly mood altering and makes you very "happy." Drug dens are now selling the tablets for R5 each - they retail from pharmacies and self dispensing doctors for around R1 each. They also sell Pax, Diasophon and Parata which has similar effects. We have found one big dealer in the Northern areas - a couple who sell large quantities out of their garage, We have access to hidden camera footage from the PE PI who has been working on the case. He's willing to hand some of it over. I have asked my fixer Riaan to place the house under surveillance and to go and do some enquiries about what is available but not to buy,



Further information:
Aspen pharmaceuticals in PE have employed investigators as has the Dept of Health to try and root out who is supplying these dealers. I have met with the Dept of Health investigator who showed me their top 4 - Dr Claasen in Gelvendale, Dr Noah, Anver Ahmed pharmacy and Korsten pharmacy, Anver Ahmed pharmacy sells aroun 172000 stipaine in one month - thats more than all the Clicks pharmacies in the Nelson Mandela Metro put together. Actually around 50000 more tablets. There are cases registered against both doctors and the PI has some footage of traps where they bought without percription.

Now you'r probably thinking so what - its just painkillers that make people happy. True, but abuse of these medicines have serious side effects - liver and kidney damage which comes at a huge cost to our already over burdened health system.

Adding yet another layer to the story - cases have been made against these Doctors and pharmacies and complaints and information handed over to the SAPS in 2007 and 2008 and yet the problem keeps growing and nothing is done. The dockets are currently sitting with Col Arries at Organised crime - he works under Col Booysen who is suspected to have links to the underworld.


Bottom line - its a cut and dried open secret, with registered cases - why are the police so reluctant to do anything?

We also have cops on standby who said they will shut down the drug den and arrest the owners as soon as we are done with our confront. We can get this on camera.

I was hoping to shoot next week 29,30 April and then edit for the following Sunday - the first week we are back.

Press Release:


Green Beans
Dependence on prescription drugs is a global phenomenon. In the US, 45 people overdose on prescription medication every day. Locally, the demand for schedule 5 medicines has grown so big that dealers have mushroomed across Port Elizabeth, some selling directly to addicts from garages. Stilpaine, known among pushers and users as ‘green beans’, is a hot favourite with women addicted to its pain-numbing qualities. But who is supplying this trade? Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


Script Green Beans


Script Green Beans

VO: 21”

Prescription drug abuse kills 45 Americans every day. There the problem is pharmacy hopping. But here in Port Elizabeth’s poverty stricken northern suburbs popular schedule 5 drugs like stilpayne pax and purata are sold in their thousands every day in drug dens and from drug posts on virtually every street corner.

John: Verkoop hulle Stilpayne hierso?

Dawn:
Hulle’s vollop hierso vollop- hulle staan so met die stilpain. Ek laaik die waarheid – ek gaan dood vir die waarheid.

Vox:
Dawn moenie lieg nie, dis nie die waarheid nie.

Dawn:
Dis die waarheid! Hey!

John:
Is it true?

Voxie:
Look at her you decide.

VO:
A hidden camera proved that Dawn was right. From behind the shebeen there’s a roaring trade.

Hidden cam:

So this is R50’s worth.
-Yes
Ok I’ll come back for the bottles.
- Ok how many bottles do you want?

VO:
Just down the road at a spaza shop they offer what amounts to a drive through service.

Drug den 2

VO:
And they deliver straight to you in a waiting car.
Hidden camera
I’m coming to buy Pax.
-How much do you want?
R40 pax and R50 worth of Stilpaine.
-R50 Stilpaine.

VO:
Alternatively you could just visit your favourite dealer in his den.

Dealer:
Die Stilpayne my broer hulle werk so R2,50 los.

- Elke een?
Ja. Dan die Stilpaine kry jy ook in R50 pakke. En R100 pakke.
- En die bottels van die stilpaine?
Dis R 900 daai.

VO:
That’s R900 for a thousand. He showed us the popular portions.


- Hoeveel is dit nou?
Dis ‘n R100 pak daai, dis ‘n order jy verstaan.

VO:
Sannie, a 53 year old grandmother is an addict.

John: Sannie vir hoe lank het jy al Stilpayne gebruik?

Sannie:
Vir 19 jaar.

John: So lank al?

Sannie:
Ja

John:
En hoeveel keer neem jy dit?
Sannie:
10 per dag?

John:
10 per dag?

Sannie: Ja.
VO: 2”
Colloquially known as green beans they are dirt cheap.
John:
Can you give us an idea of how much it costs
Sannie?

Sannie:
R1 each.

John:
R1 each. So its costing you around R10 a day

VO:
It’s a growing trend according to Roger Weimann who runs the Eastern cape branch of SANCA – he says it increases month on month.

Roger:
The amount that is on the street is alarmingly high and we’re seeing it become more and more so.

VO:
Even more sinister is the emergence of a new deadly drug Krokodil …. Originating in Russia in 2002 when their laws governing codeine were lax the drug is made of codeine opiates mixed with paint thinners or gasoline and a few other products you rather would not inject. It’s known as the flesh eating drug that’s more addictive than heroine and comes in at a tenth of the price. It’s name krokodil comes from the scales and rough skin caused by injecting the drug – often these lesions become gangrenous. The death toll is high.
With an almost endless supply of stilpayne on the streets concerns are mounting that the drug will take hold. Ivan Kotze of the Pharmacy society believes we need to close the gap.

Ivan:
We share your concern, really the substance should not be freely available and that’s the intention of the legislation. And that’s the function of the professionals, pharmacists and doctors to ensure that it does not end up in the market to be abused.

VO: 19
It’s easy to see why the drug is seducing its first victims here, like in the slums of Russia the demand is driven by poverty and a sense of desperation. People here use drugs to numb themselves to their circumstances. For Sannie she started using stilpayne when her relationship with her husband hit the skids.

Sannie:
Toe my man begin h**r toe sit die doctor my op dit.

VO: 3
It soon became a fully fledged addiction.

Sannie:
Dit maak my stil, dit maak my rustig. Maar as ek nugter is, as ek dit nie gebruik nie, dan praat ek dinge wat ek wou se wat ek lankal inhou. Wanneer ek dit in my system het dan is ek stil, dan laat ek alles maar verby gaan.


VO: 14”
The Aspen pharmacy that manufacture Stilpayne pax and purata the 3 psychotrophic drugs commonly sold here is just down the road near the stadium. But Aspen executive Stavros Nicholaou says the drugs are not coming directly from their factory.

Stavros:
We’re pretty confident in fact that the problem does not come from within Aspen or from the employees of Aspen working at that particular site.

VO: 2’5”
He says their numbers all add up.

Stavros:
Our point of control is from the point that we receive the raw material to convert it into the finished product up until where we deliver it to our warehouse and that all reconciles.

VO:
So if they aren’t coming from the factory – who is supplying them? A local dealer Johnny agreed to meet with us.

Johnny:
So I’d say the majority of them are doctors, policemen. Basically policemen because everything works through them. Without the police you wouldn’t be able to sell drugs.

John
So just for clarity you’re getting your drugs through police officers is that right?

Johnny:
No not actually – they escort your shipment in and then there you go. And then it lands on the street, people who are meant to cure you, they are the people who are doing the wrong things.

John:
So just tell me if I have this right Johnny, the doctors are getting the prescription drugs, they are supplying the dealers and those drugs are getting into the areas for distribution with the help of police?

Johnny. That’s correct yes.

VO:
We approached the local police spokesman Warrant Officer Alwin Labans to explain.

John:
An allegation that keeps coming up in the interviews that we have had with drug users, with dealers with members of the public is that police are complicit, they’re involved.

Alwin.
If that is the case, people have to come forward to the police, we are rooting out all our bad cops, we investigate them, we do have the capacity to do that, and if police are doing that we will book them.

VO:
The dealer’s allegations about doctors tied in with information we’d received.

Link:
We spoke to an investigator with detailed knowledge of the problem – the figures he provided us with were shocking and pointed to the involvement of rogue doctors and pharmacists. The question is whose job is it to investigate them?

Ivan:
It’s department of health officials that does the inspections.

VO: 15
In one case where as our investigator showed us the register reflected that one pharmacist had sold 172000 tablets substantially more than the average 10 000 sold at other pharmacies in the metro. Surely this should have raised a red flag?

Ivan:
I think that’s where the investigation should start and work back from there. Pharmacies should be able to show that there are indeed legal prescriptions for that amount of product being supplied.


VO: 7”
It’s heartbreaking that the same doctors and pharmacies meant to be the custodians of our healthcare system could be supplying gateway drugs. 16 yo Ricardo started taking prescription drugs when he was just 12.

Ricardo:
It first began with Ritalin and it put me on a trip. Then I started taking stilpaine at home and that also put me on a trip. Then I looked for something stronger so I started taking heroin and mandrax and dagga. Toe begin ek tik te rook.

VO: 6
Four years later he’s a hardened addict who will do anything for his next fix.

Ricardo:
I stole at my father’s house.

John:
So you steal from your dad.

Ricardo:
Yes.

VO: 10”
Three weeks ago things came to a head when his father Frank had to rescue him from dealers who he owed money.

Frank:
He wasn’t sober he was on a high. So I took him home and that evening I took him to the police station and I had him arrested.

John:
It’s quite a tough thing to do – why did you decide on that course of action?

Frank:
Because that would be the safest for him – when he stole the last bit of stuff from me after we let him free he went back to this drug dealer and when he got to them he didn’t have enough money on him and they beat him up and where else could he go and so I said best for you behind bars to keep him safe.


VO: 7”
These same doctors and pharmacies who are alleged to be selling to dealers are also turning a blind eye to the side effects of the abuse.

Roger:
You get a lot of liver damage, kidney damage, high blood pressure and that places a huge burden on the health system.

VO: 17”
With dialysis costing around R200 000 per patient per year it will place strain on the already cash strapped provincial healthcare department.

VO:
The police say they are doing their best to clamp down.

Labans:
We have our crime prevention units, our drug task teams as well as some gang task team guys that’s doing these raids daily.

VO: 7
Upsound – banging “Maak oop die deur”

A recent joint operation Project Fiela targeting Raids project Fiela aimed at illegals also netted some pharmaceuticals.

Drug den 1 VO: 5”
We returned to the drug dens who had been caught selling on camera, At the first drug den people started disappearing the minute we arrived.

John:
John from Carte Blanche how are you?

Drug den visitor:
Carte Blanche – channel 101.

John:
That’s the one. We have some footage of drugs being sold from here.

Visitor:
I don’t know about it.

John:
Is there anybody here who works here?

Visitor:
There is but he’s working over there.

John:
Can you call him for us please?
VO:
Needless to say the manager never made an appearance

Drug den 2 VO: 8”
At the second drug den which doubled as a spaza shop– owner Eric spoke to us from behind his door.

Upsound drug den 1

John: Stilpaine is one of the tablets that apparently is very popular. Do you know anything about that?
You seem unsure now Eric?

Eric:
That was way back when.


John link:
One of the obstacles to clamping down on this scourge is what our insider calls small town syndrome – all the people in the chain from the doctors to the police officers to the dealers themselves know each other and that’s why these cases appear to go nowhere.

VO:
Government is now in the process of setting up a new drug authority SAPRA to stem the tide.

Ivan:
The current medicines control council will be replaced by a new drug authority SAPRA – once of the objectives is very clearly an active inspection programme.

Vo: 5”
Stavros wants to see a track and trace programme for scheduled drugs implemented.

Stavros:
I think what we have to do is assist them and give them systems help them root out the illicit trade that’s taking place.

VO: 3”
In the interim our addicts need help.

John:
So you want to stop?

Sannie:
I really want to stop.

VO: 4
Ricardo visited SANCA the day after our interview with his father.

Frank
I’ve got hope that its going to work, I don’t know what it entails but I know people who have been here at SANCA who have recovered from using drugs.

VO: 13”
Ricardo met with social workers and was booked into their outpatients programme.


VO:
He’s one of the lucky ones – we hope it breaks his cycle of abuse. Thousands of others go untreated in the silent epidemic that’s stalking our suburbs.


Promo 1: 10 sec

VO: 5
Prescription drugs sold in their thousands in drug dens.

John: Verkoop hulle Stilpayne hierso?

Dawn: Dis vollop…dit staan so.


Promo 2: 15 sec

VO:
Codeine based drugs mixed with paint thinners or petrol is used to make a new deadly flesh eating drug called krokodil.

Ivan: share your concern

VO:
The first cases have surfaced in Port Elizabeth.


Promo 3: 15 sec

VO: 6”
Undercover footage of prescription drugs sold in PE’s drugdens – they even offer a drive through service.

Upsound hidden cam

VO: 2
And deliver straight to your car.

VO: That’s R900 for a thousand. He showed us the popular portions. - Hoeveel is dit nou? Dis ‘n R100 pak daai, dis ‘n order jy verstaan. VO: Sannie, a 53 year old grandmother is an addict. John: Sannie vir hoe lank het jy al Stilpayne gebruik? Sannie: Vir 19 jaar. John: So lank al? Sannie: Ja John: En hoeveel keer neem jy dit? Sannie: 10 per dag? John: 10 per dag? Sannie: Ja. VO: 2” Colloquially known as green beans they are dirt cheap. John: Can you give us an idea of how much it costs Sannie? Sannie: R1 each. John: R1 each. So its costing you around R10 a day VO: It’s a growing trend according to Roger Weimann who runs the Eastern cape branch of SANCA – he says it increases month on month. Roger: The amount that is on the street is alarmingly high and we’re seeing it become more and more so. VO: Even more sinister is the emergence of a new deadly drug Krokodil …. Originating in Russia in 2002 when their laws governing codeine were lax the drug is made of codeine opiates mixed with paint thinners or gasoline and a few other products you rather would not inject. It’s known as the flesh eating drug that’s more addictive than heroine and comes in at a tenth of the price. It’s name krokodil comes from the scales and rough skin caused by injecting the drug – often these lesions become gangrenous. The death toll is high. With an almost endless supply of stilpayne on the streets concerns are mounting that the drug will take hold. Ivan Kotze of the Pharmacy society believes we need to close the gap. Ivan: We share your concern, really the substance should not be freely available and that’s the intention of the legislation. And that’s the function of the professionals, pharmacists and doctors to ensure that it does not end up in the market to be abused. VO: 19 It’s easy to see why the drug is seducing its first victims here, like in the slums of Russia the demand is driven by poverty and a sense of desperation. People here use drugs to numb themselves to their circumstances. For Sannie she started using stilpayne when her relationship with her husband hit the skids. Sannie: Toe my man begin h**r toe sit die doctor my op dit. VO: 3 It soon became a fully fledged addiction. Sannie: Dit maak my stil, dit maak my rustig. Maar as ek nugter is, as ek dit nie gebruik nie, dan praat ek dinge wat ek wou se wat ek lankal inhou. Wanneer ek dit in my system het dan is ek stil, dan laat ek alles maar verby gaan. VO: 14” The Aspen pharmacy that manufacture Stilpayne pax and purata the 3 psychotrophic drugs commonly sold here is just down the road near the stadium. But Aspen executive Stavros Nicholaou says the drugs are not coming directly from their factory. Stavros: We’re pretty confident in fact that the problem does not come from within Aspen or from the employees of Aspen working at that particular site. VO: 2’5” He says their numbers all add up. Stavros: Our point of control is from the point that we receive the raw material to convert it into the finished product up until where we deliver it to our warehouse and that all reconciles. VO: So if they aren’t coming from the factory – who is supplying them? A local dealer Johnny agreed to meet with us. Johnny: So I’d say the majority of them are doctors, policemen. Basically policemen because everything works through them. Without the police you wouldn’t be able to sell drugs. John So just for clarity you’re getting your drugs through police officers is that right? Johnny: No not actually – they escort your shipment in and then there you go. And then it lands on the street, people who are meant to cure you, they are the people who are doing the wrong things. John: So just tell me if I have this right Johnny, the doctors are getting the prescription drugs, they are supplying the dealers and those drugs are getting into the areas for distribution with the help of police? Johnny. That’s correct yes. VO: We approached the local police spokesman Warrant Officer Alwin Labans to explain. John: An allegation that keeps coming up in the interviews that we have had with drug users, with dealers with members of the public is that police are complicit, they’re involved. Alwin. If that is the case, people have to come forward to the police, we are rooting out all our bad cops, we investigate them, we do have the capacity to do that, and if police are doing that we will book them. VO: The dealer’s allegations about doctors tied in with information we’d received. Link: We spoke to an investigator with detailed knowledge of the problem – the figures he provided us with were shocking and pointed to the involvement of rogue doctors and pharmacists. The question is whose job is it to investigate them? Ivan: It’s department of health officials that does the inspections. VO: 15 In one case where as our investigator showed us the register reflected that one pharmacist had sold 172000 tablets substantially more than the average 10 000 sold at other pharmacies in the metro. Surely this should have raised a red flag? Ivan: I think that’s where the investigation should start and work back from there. Pharmacies should be able to show that there are indeed legal prescriptions for that amount of product being supplied. VO: 7” It’s heartbreaking that the same doctors and pharmacies meant to be the custodians of our healthcare system could be supplying gateway drugs. 16 yo Ricardo started taking prescription drugs when he was just 12. Ricardo: It first began with Ritalin and it put me on a trip. Then I started taking stilpaine at home and that also put me on a trip. Then I looked for something stronger so I started taking heroin and mandrax and dagga. Toe begin ek tik te rook. VO: 6 Four years later he’s a hardened addict who will do anything for his next fix. Ricardo: I stole at my father’s house. John: So you steal from your dad. Ricardo: Yes. VO: 10” Three weeks ago things came to a head when his father Frank had to rescue him from dealers who he owed money. Frank: He wasn’t sober he was on a high. So I took him home and that evening I took him to the police station and I had him arrested. John: It’s quite a tough thing to do – why did you decide on that course of action? Frank: Because that would be the safest for him – when he stole the last bit of stuff from me after we let him free he went back to this drug dealer and when he got to them he didn’t have enough money on him and they beat him up and where else could he go and so I said best for you behind bars to keep him safe. VO: 7” These same doctors and pharmacies who are alleged to be selling to dealers are also turning a blind eye to the side effects of the abuse. Roger: You get a lot of liver damage, kidney damage, high blood pressure and that places a huge burden on the health system. VO: 17” With dialysis costing around R200 000 per patient per year it will place strain on the already cash strapped provincial healthcare department. VO: The police say they are doing their best to clamp down. Labans: We have our crime prevention units, our drug task teams as well as some gang task team guys that’s doing these raids daily. VO: 7 Upsound – banging “Maak oop die deur” A recent joint operation Project Fiela targeting Raids project Fiela aimed at illegals also netted some pharmaceuticals. Drug den 1 VO: 5” We returned to the drug dens who had been caught selling on camera, At the first drug den people started disappearing the minute we arrived. John: John from Carte Blanche how are you? Drug den visitor: Carte Blanche – channel 101. John: That’s the one. We have some footage of drugs being sold from here. Visitor: I don’t know about it. John: Is there anybody here who works here? Visitor: There is but he’s working over there. John: Can you call him for us please? VO: Needless to say the manager never made an appearance Drug den 2 VO: 8” At the second drug den which doubled as a spaza shop– owner Eric spoke to us from behind his door. Upsound drug den 1 John: Stilpaine is one of the tablets that apparently is very popular. Do you know anything about that? You seem unsure now Eric? Eric: That was way back when. John link: One of the obstacles to clamping down on this scourge is what our insider calls small town syndrome – all the people in the chain from the doctors to the police officers to the dealers themselves know each other and that’s why these cases appear to go nowhere. VO: Government is now in the process of setting up a new drug authority SAPRA to stem the tide. Ivan: The current medicines control council will be replaced by a new drug authority SAPRA – once of the objectives is very clearly an active inspection programme. Vo: 5” Stavros wants to see a track and trace programme for scheduled drugs implemented. Stavros: I think what we have to do is assist them and give them systems help them root out the illicit trade that’s taking place. VO: 3” In the interim our addicts need help. John: So you want to stop? Sannie: I really want to stop. VO: 4 Ricardo visited SANCA the day after our interview with his father. Frank I’ve got hope that its going to work, I don’t know what it entails but I know people who have been here at SANCA who have recovered from using drugs. VO: 13” Ricardo met with social workers and was booked into their outpatients programme. VO: He’s one of the lucky ones – we hope it breaks his cycle of abuse. Thousands of others go untreated in the silent epidemic that’s stalking our suburbs. Promo 1: 10 sec VO: 5 Prescription drugs sold in their thousands in drug dens. John: Verkoop hulle Stilpayne hierso? Dawn: Dis vollop…dit staan so. Promo 2: 15 sec VO: Codeine based drugs mixed with paint thinners or petrol is used to make a new deadly flesh eating drug called krokodil. Ivan: share your concern VO: The first cases have surfaced in Port Elizabeth. Promo 3: 15 sec VO: 6” Undercover footage of prescription drugs sold in PE’s drugdens – they even offer a drive through service. Upsound hidden cam VO: 2 And deliver straight to your car.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Drug dens are expanding their offering to include mood altering and psyhotrophic schedule 5 medicines. We investigate who the doctors and pharmacies are behind the trend.
metadata.Summary: Stilpaine is known in the northern areas of PE as "green beans." The schedule 5 pain killer is in high demand. A few tablets taken with alcohol is reportedly mood altering and makes you very "happy." Drug dens are now selling the tablets for R5 each - they retail from pharmacies and self dispensing doctors for around R1 each. They also sell Pax, Diasophon and Parata which has similar effects. We have found one big dealer in the Northern areas - a couple who sell large quantities out of their garage, We have access to hidden camera footage from the PE PI who has been working on the case. He's willing to hand some of it over. I have asked my fixer Riaan to place the house under surveillance and to go and do some enquiries about what is available but not to buy,
metadata.Further information: Aspen pharmaceuticals in PE have employed investigators as has the Dept of Health to try and root out who is supplying these dealers. I have met with the Dept of Health investigator who showed me their top 4 - Dr Claasen in Gelvendale, Dr Noah, Anver Ahmed pharmacy and Korsten pharmacy, Anver Ahmed pharmacy sells aroun 172000 stipaine in one month - thats more than all the Clicks pharmacies in the Nelson Mandela Metro put together. Actually around 50000 more tablets. There are cases registered against both doctors and the PI has some footage of traps where they bought without percription. Now you'r probably thinking so what - its just painkillers that make people happy. True, but abuse of these medicines have serious side effects - liver and kidney damage which comes at a huge cost to our already over burdened health system. Adding yet another layer to the story - cases have been made against these Doctors and pharmacies and complaints and information handed over to the SAPS in 2007 and 2008 and yet the problem keeps growing and nothing is done. The dockets are currently sitting with Col Arries at Organised crime - he works under Col Booysen who is suspected to have links to the underworld. Bottom line - its a cut and dried open secret, with registered cases - why are the police so reluctant to do anything? We also have cops on standby who said they will shut down the drug den and arrest the owners as soon as we are done with our confront. We can get this on camera. I was hoping to shoot next week 29,30 April and then edit for the following Sunday - the first week we are back.
